newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Old silver coin raises riddle of Australian history.
newsitem.headline: Old silver coin raises riddle of Australian history.

text.p: An Australian beachcomber has reignited debate about the nation's early history by unearthing an old silver coin said to have been dropped by a Portuguese mariner almost 500 years ago on the continent's southeast coast.

The find, made in September but only publicised on Friday after initial checks of the coin's antiquity, is seen as perhaps the first tangible evidence to support a contentious theory that the Portuguese were the first to chart eastern Australia.

Australian children are taught that Britain's Captain James Cook was the first European to explore the continent's east coast in 1770, about 250 years after the coin was thought to be dropped on the foreshore near Melbourne.
Cook, who claimed the east coast for Britain, paved the way for the colonisation of the east coast from 1788 where today the overwhelming majority of Australians still live.

The badly worn coin was found using a metal detector beneath about 30 cm (a foot) of soil by a beachcomber who sought anonymity but told local media he had sent the coin to an expert in Lisbon and was now awaiting the final word on its authenticity.

"This is the first material piece of evidence which you can handle and it therefore is of very, very great importance," said historian Kenneth Gordon McIntyre, author of "The Secret Discovery of Australia".
McIntyre, who has studied photographs of the coin, told Reuters it bore distinctive symbols such as a Christian cross rendered in the Portuguese style.
It was found on coastline McIntyre claims was mapped in the 1520s by Portuguese explorer Cristovao de Mendonca.
"My opinion is that it's Portuguese," McIntyre said.
A coin export with Melbourne's Museum of Victoria, John Sharples, said on Friday the coin could be a copy but agreed the artefact needed to be examined further.
"If it's not very high-quality silver, then it's definitely a copy," Sharples told state radio.

McIntyre's thesis relies mainly on old Portuguese maps which he says shows de Mendonca sailed down the continent's east coast and into Bass Strait, where the coin was found, at a time when Portugal and Spain had divided the world between them.
McIntyre has been knighted by the Portuguese government for his research, but has yet to find any material evidence of a Portuguese presence so far east.

He claims one of Mendonca's ships wrecked on the southeast coast, but all attempts to find the remains of the so-called "Mahogany Ship" have failed, despite a A$250,000 reward offered by the Victoria state government in 1993.
